title: Al-Wadud, the Loving
hook: the Loving, whose love is steady and shown

segments.voice: Yesterday, Al-Halim, the Forbearing, who doesn't rush to punish. Your line was slow to anger. Did you catch one breath between the sting and the answer? Day two hundred fifty-one.

Some people never say I love you. A father who gets up at five to scrape the ice off your windshield before you're awake. A grandmother who remembers you hate onions and quietly picks them out of your plate for thirty years. A friend who shows up to help you move and doesn't mention it again. You know the love, not because anyone said it, but because it keeps showing up, in the same shape, over and over. Arabic has more than one word for love, and one of them is exactly this: love that shows. Love you can see in what it does. The Qur'an uses it as a name of God. Today: Al-Wadud.
screen: `ICE SCRAPED OFF THE WINDSHIELD.` → `NO ONIONS, FOR THIRTY YEARS.` → `LOVE THAT SHOWS.`

segments.voice: Al-Wadud comes from wudd. Arabic's everyday word for love is hubb. Scholars of the language describe wudd as love that comes out, that is expressed and felt, steady affection you can see. So al-Wadud is not only the One who loves, but the One whose love is shown, and keeps being shown. The name appears twice in the Qur'an, and both times it's paired with forgiveness. In one, the prophet Shu'ayb tells his people to ask forgiveness and turn back, because his Lord is merciful and loving. In the other, in Surah al-Buruj, in Pickthall's words: "And He is the Forgiving, the Loving." Notice the order. Forgiveness first, then love. Classical scholars noticed it too: God doesn't forgive grudgingly and then keep his distance. He forgives, and then loves. Another verse says that for those who believe and do good, the Merciful will make love, wudd, the same word, for them. And a hadith in Sahih al-Bukhari tells how that love travels. When God loves a servant, he calls the angel Gabriel and tells him, I love this person, so love them. Gabriel loves them, and calls out to the heavens, and the heavens love them. And then acceptance is set down for them on the earth. People start to feel it, without knowing why. So the name has two sides. God's love is shown: steady, like the ice scraper at five a.m. And a person can be wadud too, by making love visible, in deeds, the way God's is.
screen: `WUDD — LOVE THAT SHOWS.` · `THE FORGIVING, THE LOVING.` · `GABRIEL, THEN THE HEAVENS, THEN EARTH.` · `LOVE MADE VISIBLE IN DEEDS.` · then, large: `LOVED.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: show love to someone in a deed. Sit for a moment and let a face come to mind, someone who'd never guess you're thinking of them. Then choose one small thing you could do for them today. Not a speech. A deed. Make the tea. Send the photo. Fix the thing that's been broken. Picture yourself doing it. And, if you pray, you can call on God as al-Wadud, the Loving. Then just sit, and let yourself be loved for a minute. The bell holds the time.
Al-Wadud. The Loving: love that is steady, and shown, not only felt. Today's word.
Your line: loved. Today, do the one deed you pictured, and don't mention it. Let it speak for itself. Day two hundred fifty-one.

howItsDone: Muslims call on God as al-Wadud in du'a, and many understand love for others as something shown in deeds: gifts, visits, help, and a hadith that says to give gifts to one another so love grows.

myth: in both its verses, al-Wadud is paired with forgiveness
Shu'ayb's merciful and loving, and al-Buruj's the Forgiving, the Loving.
wudd and hubb mean exactly the same thing
wudd is love that comes out and is shown; hubb is the everyday word.
in the hadith, love for a person begins on earth and rises to heaven
it runs the other way: God, then Gabriel, then the heavens, then acceptance on earth.

fork.setup: in the hadith, God loves a servant. who does he tell first?
fork.reveal: Gabriel, who loves them too and calls to the heavens; then acceptance is set down for them on the earth.

original.note: Arabic: the Loving. from wudd, love that is shown.

trapdoor: what you thought: God loves everyone, in general.
what it means: the Loving, whose love is steady and shown, who forgives and then draws close.
what a scholar hears: wudd, not hubb: lexicographers describe it as affection made visible. both Qur'anic uses (11:90, 85:14) pair it with forgiveness.
